rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wind image depicts disbelievers' actions in this life as unrooted and sterile.
rows.anchor: how unrooted and sterile the actions of disbelievers are in this life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's cold wind contrasts with the burning wind in 2:266; 14:18 depicts disbelievers' deeds as ashes ready to blow away.
rows.anchor: the wind is cold, while in 2:266 it burns, and in 14:18 the deeds of disbelievers are already ashes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere wind also has a nourishing dimension, as in 7:57, 25:48, 30:46, and 35:9.
rows.anchor: Verses involving the nourishing dimension of wind include 7:57; 25:48; 30:46; 35:9.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly speaks of people wronging themselves.
rows.anchor: The wronging of oneself is mentioned numerous times in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning is interpreted as applying to the hoarding of both material wealth and spiritual knowledge.
rows.anchor: This verse is interpreted to refer to the hoarding of both material wealth and spiritual knowledge

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ identifies those withholding spiritual knowledge as the People of the Book, who refused to teach the scripture they possessed.
rows.anchor: those who did not share spiritual knowledge are the People of the Book, because they refused to teach the Book they had (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of being collared by what one withheld resembles the warning about fraud in 3:161.
rows.anchor: The imagery of being collared by what one withheld is similar to the imagery in v. 161

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says a miser's hoard appears at Judgment as a serpent that consumes or coils around him and identifies itself as his wealth and treasure; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: Among the interpretations attributed to the Prophet for this verse is that a person’s hoard of wealth will appear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The harmful effects of miserliness are also treated in 4:37, 47:37–38, and 57:24.
rows.anchor: The deleterious effects of miserliness are also discussed in 4:37; 47:37–38; 57:24.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's conclusion resembles 19:40, where God says He will inherit the earth and all upon it.
rows.anchor: The end of this verse is similar to 19:40: We shall inherit the earth

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Commentators distinguish God's inheritance from human inheritance: God always possesses the heavens and earth, and inherits them when all other owners cease to exist and He alone remains.
rows.anchor: all other owners cease to be and He alone remains (Q, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: It is said that the Prophet recited verses 190–200 of this sūrah every night.
rows.anchor: the Prophet would recite vv. 190–200 of this sūrah every night

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A report says Bilāl found the praying Prophet weeping when these verses were first revealed; asked why despite forgiveness, he answered that he should be a grateful servant and warned against reciting without reflection.
rows.anchor: the Prophet stood to pray, and while he was praying Bilāl came to call him to the congregational prayer, found him weeping

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims are advised to read the verse and meditate deeply on its meanings, including their levels.
rows.anchor: Muslims are therefore advised not only to read, but also to meditate deeply upon the meanings—in fact, levels of meaning—of this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalq can mean God's creative act or the created nature and qualities of the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: khalq, which can refer not only to God’s creative Act, but also to the nature or qualities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variation of night and day is also discussed in 2:164, 10:6, 23:80, and 45:5; 2:164 also mentions creation of the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: On the variation of the night and the day, see also 2:164

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion of possessors of intellect (ūlu’l-albāb) is linked to 2:179, 39:9, 13:19, 14:52, 38:29, and 39:18.
